sections.title: How to use these notes
sections.html:
The 2024/25 PHY112 final (Geometrical Optics and Mechanics) has 10 questions; you answer any 8, 10 marks each, 80 marks, 120 minutes. Every question below maps to one topic, and each topic section ends with that question fully worked.

Q Topic What it really tests
1 Dimensional analysis Dimensions of pressure and density; adding only like terms
2 Vectors in 2D Components when the angle is from the x-axis vs the y-axis; direction of a resultant
3 Cross product A vector perpendicular to two vectors = their cross product
4 Projectile motion Time to reach a wall, then height at that time
5 Newton's laws, friction Free-body diagrams and connected masses on a rough incline
6 Apparent weight; work-energy Scale reading in an accelerating lift; v from energy
7 Momentum and collisions Conservation of momentum; elastic test with kinetic energy
8 Plane mirrors Image properties; images between two facing mirrors
9 Spherical mirrors Mirror equation, magnification, sign convention
10 Refraction n = c/v, Snell's law, apparent depth

Exam rules from the cover page: g = 9.8 m/s², c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, round non-exact final answers to one decimal place, and for small angles sin θ ≈ tan θ (used in Q10).

Strategy for picking 8: Q1, Q3, Q7 and Q9 are pure method and the safest marks. Q8(b) and Q10(c) need a clear sketch; practise them so they become safe too. Your labs already covered Q5 (Incline Friction Lab, Newton's Laws page), Q6 (Elevator Overload Lab) and Q7 (Ballistic Pendulum: momentum conserved, energy not).

Every numerical answer in these notes was checked twice: once by hand and once by an independent method (dot-product check, substitution, or energy check).

sections.title: Units and dimensional analysis (Q1)
sections.html:
An equation is dimensionally correct when every term on both sides has the same dimensions. Write each quantity in terms of M (mass), L (length) and T (time), then compare.

Rules

  • You can only add or subtract quantities with the same dimensions. Check each term separately.
  • Pure numbers (2, ½, π) and angles are dimensionless, so they disappear.
  • (P − P₀) has the same dimensions as P.
  • Dimensional analysis cannot detect a wrong number (2 instead of ½). A correct check means "consistent", not "definitely physically true". Say this for the last mark.

Dimensions to memorise

Quantity Formula used Dimensions SI unit
Velocity distance / time L T⁻¹ m/s
Acceleration, g velocity / time L T⁻² m/s²
Force ma M L T⁻² N
Momentum, impulse mv M L T⁻¹ kg·m/s
Work, energy Fd M L² T⁻² J
Power work / time M L² T⁻³ W
Pressure force / area M L⁻¹ T⁻² Pa
Density, ρ mass / volume M L⁻³ kg/m³
Spring constant, k F / x M T⁻² N/m
Frequency 1 / time T⁻¹ Hz
Gravitational constant, G Fr² / (m₁m₂) M⁻¹ L³ T⁻² N·m²/kg²

Method (5 steps for full marks)

  1. Write the dimensions of every symbol, showing where they come from (e.g. pressure = force/area).
  2. Find the dimensions of each term on the right separately.
  3. Show the terms you add have the same dimensions.
  4. Simplify the right-hand side (square roots halve the powers).
  5. Compare with the left-hand side and state the conclusion in words.

WorkedQ1 worked: v = √(2(P − P₀)/ρ + 2gh)

  • [v] = L T⁻¹
  • [P − P₀] = M L T⁻² / L² = M L⁻¹ T⁻²
  • [ρ] = M L⁻³
  • First term: (M L⁻¹ T⁻²) / (M L⁻³) = L² T⁻²
  • Second term: [g][h] = (L T⁻²)(L) = L² T⁻²
  • Both terms are L² T⁻², so adding them is valid.
  • RHS = √(L² T⁻²) = L T⁻¹ = LHS.

Conclusion: the equation is dimensionally correct. (It is a form of Bernoulli's equation.)

Variations to expect: check s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, T = 2π√(L/g), T = 2π√(m/k) from your spring lab, or find the power n in an equation such as v = k gⁿ hᵐ by matching powers of M, L and T.

checks.q: What are the dimensions of pressure?
checks.x: Pressure = force / area = (M L T⁻²) / L² = M L⁻¹ T⁻².

checks.q: A spring constant is k = F / x. What are its dimensions?
checks.x: (M L T⁻²) / L = M T⁻². The L cancels.

checks.q: Which mistake can dimensional analysis NOT catch?
o: Writing 2 instead of ½ in front of a term
Adding a speed to an acceleration
Using L² where L is needed
Leaving out a factor of time
checks.x: Pure numbers are dimensionless, so a wrong constant leaves the dimensions unchanged. A correct check means consistent, not definitely true.

sections.title: Vectors in 2D (Q2)
sections.html:
A vector has magnitude and direction. Break every vector into x and y components, do the arithmetic component by component, then rebuild the magnitude and angle.

Components: the one rule that saves marks

  • Angle measured from the x-axis: x uses cos, y uses sin. Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ.
  • Angle measured from the y-axis: swap them. Bₓ = B sin θ, Bᵧ = B cos θ.
  • Then give each component its sign from the quadrant it points into.
Quadrant Points Sign of x Sign of y
1st up-right + +
2nd up-left − +
3rd down-left − −
4th down-right + −

Unit vectors: î along +x, ĵ along +y, k̂ along +z, each of length 1. A vector is written A = Aₓî + Aᵧĵ.

Adding, subtracting, scaling: add matching components. kA multiplies every component by k. A − 2B = (Aₓ − 2Bₓ)î + (Aᵧ − 2Bᵧ)ĵ.

Magnitude and direction of R = Rₓî + Rᵧĵ

  • |R| = √(Rₓ² + Rᵧ²)
  • Reference angle α = tan⁻¹(|Rᵧ| / |Rₓ|), always between 0° and 90°.
  • Angle from the +x axis: 1st quadrant θ = α; 2nd θ = 180° − α; 3rd θ = 180° + α; 4th θ = 360° − α.
  • Never trust the calculator's tan⁻¹ on its own; it cannot tell 2nd from 4th quadrant. Sketch first.

WorkedQ2 worked: |A| = 15 at 40° above the −x axis, |B| = 10 at 20° from the −y axis, C = A − 2B

(a) A points up-left (2nd quadrant), angle from the x-axis: A = −15 cos 40° î + 15 sin 40° ĵ = −11.5î + 9.6ĵ

B points down-left (3rd quadrant), angle from the y-axis, so sin goes with x: B = −10 sin 20° î − 10 cos 20° ĵ = −3.4î − 9.4ĵ

(b) 2B = −6.84î − 18.79ĵ C = (−11.49 + 6.84)î + (9.64 + 18.79)ĵ = −4.7î + 28.4ĵ

(c) Sketch C in the 2nd quadrant, long and leaning slightly left of the +y axis. |C| = √(4.65² + 28.44²) = 28.8 units α = tan⁻¹(28.44 / 4.65) = 80.7°, so θ = 180° − 80.7° = 99.3° from the +x axis.

Check: 99.3° is just past 90°, which matches a vector pointing almost straight up and slightly left.

checks.q: A vector of size A makes angle θ with the y-axis. What is its x-component (before signs)?
checks.x: When the angle is from the y-axis the roles swap: x uses sin, y uses cos.

checks.q: R = −3î + 4ĵ. What is its direction measured from the +x axis?
checks.x: Reference angle tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1°. R points up-left (2nd quadrant), so θ = 180° − 53.1° = 126.9°. |R| = 5.

checks.q: A vector points down and to the left. Which signs do its components have?
checks.x: Down-left is the 3rd quadrant: both components negative.

sections.title: Dot and cross products (Q3)
sections.html:
A vector perpendicular to two vectors is their cross product. The dot product is how you prove it.

Dot (scalar) product: the answer is a number

  • A · B = AₓBₓ + AᵧBᵧ + A_zB_z = |A||B| cos θ
  • A · B = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
  • Angle between two vectors: cos θ = (A · B) / (|A||B|)
  • î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 and î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0
  • Physics use: work W = F · d.

Cross (vector) product: the answer is a vector

  • |A × B| = |A||B| sin θ, pointing perpendicular to both A and B (right-hand rule).
  • A × B = −(B × A). Order matters.
  • î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ (cycle forwards = +, backwards = −). î × î = 0.
  • Physics use: torque τ = r × F.

Work it out with the determinant (expand along the top row; the middle term gets a minus sign):

\[\vec A\times\vec B=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\A_x&A_y&A_z\\B_x&B_y&B_z\end{vmatrix}=(A_yB_z-A_zB_y)\,\hat i-(A_xB_z-A_zB_x)\,\hat j+(A_xB_y-A_yB_x)\,\hat k\]

WorkedQ3 worked: D = 2î + 4ĵ − k̂, E = −3î + 5ĵ − 7k̂

  1. î: (4)(−7) − (−1)(5) = −28 + 5 = −23
  2. ĵ: −[(2)(−7) − (−1)(−3)] = −[−14 − 3] = +17
  3. k̂: (2)(5) − (4)(−3) = 10 + 12 = 22

D × E = −23î + 17ĵ + 22k̂

Prove it (always do this, it earns marks and catches sign errors)

  • (D × E) · D = (−23)(2) + (17)(4) + (22)(−1) = −46 + 68 − 22 = 0 ✓
  • (D × E) · E = (−23)(−3) + (17)(5) + (22)(−7) = 69 + 85 − 154 = 0 ✓

Both dot products are zero, so the vector is perpendicular to D and E.

The question says "one of the vectors": E × D = 23î − 17ĵ − 22k̂, or any multiple, is also correct. If asked for a unit vector: |D × E| = √(529 + 289 + 484) = √1302 = 36.1, so n̂ = (−23î + 17ĵ + 22k̂) / 36.1.

Likely extra parts: angle between D and E. D · E = −6 + 20 + 7 = 21, |D| = √21 = 4.58, |E| = √83 = 9.11, so cos θ = 21 / 41.7 and θ = 59.8°.

checks.x: Multiply matching components and add: (2)(4) + (3)(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5. A dot product is a number.

checks.q: What is ĵ × î?
checks.x: Forwards round the cycle î → ĵ → k̂ gives +. ĵ × î goes backwards, so it is −k̂.

checks.q: A · B = 0 for two non-zero vectors. What does this tell you?
o: One of them is a unit vector
checks.x: A · B = |A||B| cos θ. It is zero when cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°.

sections.title: Projectile motion (Q4)
sections.html:
Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately; time is the only thing they share. Horizontally there is no force (air resistance ignored), so the speed is constant. Vertically the acceleration is g downwards.

Equations (take up as positive, so a = −g)

Horizontal Vertical
Initial velocity uₓ = u cos θ uᵧ = u sin θ
Acceleration 0 −g
Velocity at time t vₓ = uₓ (constant) vᵧ = uᵧ − gt
Position at time t x = uₓt y = y₀ + uᵧt − ½gt²

Standard results (launched from and landing on the same level)

  • Time to the top: t = u sin θ / g. At the top vᵧ = 0, but vₓ is not zero.
  • Maximum height above launch: H = u² sin² θ / (2g)
  • Time of flight: T = 2u sin θ / g
  • Range: R = u² sin 2θ / g, largest at 45°.
  • Fired horizontally (as in your ballistic pendulum Part ii): uᵧ = 0, so H = ½gt² and R = v₀t, giving v₀ = R√(g / 2H).

"Does it hit the window?" method

  1. Use the horizontal distance to find the time: t = distance / uₓ.
  2. Put that t into y = y₀ + uᵧt − ½gt² to get the height at the wall.
  3. Compare with the window's bottom and top heights, and say clearly which way it goes.

WorkedQ4 worked: girl 2.5 m from the house, ball thrown from 1.4 m at 5 m/s, 60° above horizontal; window from 0.6 m to 1.6 m

(a) Sketch: ground line; the girl's release point 1.4 m up; the house wall 2.5 m away; window marked from 0.60 m to 1.60 m (0.60 + 1.0) on the wall; a parabola from the release point to the wall.

(b) uₓ = 5 cos 60° = 2.5 m/s; uᵧ = 5 sin 60° = 4.3 m/s (4.33)

(c) t = 2.5 / 2.5 = 1.0 s

(d) Height at the wall: y = 1.4 + (4.33)(1.0) − ½(9.8)(1.0)² = 1.4 + 4.33 − 4.9 = 0.83 m

The window runs from 0.60 m to 1.60 m, and 0.60 < 0.83 < 1.60, so the ball hits the window, about 0.23 m above its base.

Check: the ball peaks at t = 4.33 / 9.8 = 0.44 s at 1.4 + 4.33² / 19.6 = 2.36 m, then comes down. At 1.0 s it is on the way down but still above the ground, so the answer is consistent.

checks.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path (no air resistance):
o: vertical velocity is zero; horizontal velocity is unchanged
checks.x: Only vᵧ becomes zero. uₓ never changes, and the acceleration is still g downwards.

checks.q: A ball rolls off a table 4.9 m high at 6.0 m/s. How far from the table does it land? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
checks.x: Fall time: 4.9 = ½(9.8)t², so t = 1.0 s. Range = uₓt = 6.0 × 1.0 = 6.0 m.

checks.q: For launch and landing on the same level, which angle gives the greatest range?
checks.x: R = u² sin 2θ / g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, so 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°.

sections.title: Newton's laws, friction and connected masses (Q5)
sections.html:
Draw a free-body diagram for each mass, write ΣF = ma along its direction of motion, then solve the equations together. This is exactly what your Incline Friction Lab and Newton's Laws pages animate.

The three laws

  1. First law: a body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net (resultant) external force acts on it. Balanced forces: ΣF = 0.
  2. Second law: ΣF = ma. The net force sets the acceleration.
  3. Third law: when A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force. The pair acts on different bodies and is the same type of force. N and mg cos θ are not a third-law pair: they act on the same block.

Forces on a block on an incline at angle θ

Force Direction Size
Weight component along the slope down the slope mg sin θ
Weight component into the slope into the surface mg cos θ
Normal reaction N out of the surface N = mg cos θ (no other perpendicular forces)
Kinetic friction against the motion fₖ = μₖN = μₖmg cos θ
Static friction (at rest) against the tendency to move fₛ ≤ μₛN
Tension T along the string same throughout a light string over a smooth pulley

Useful lab results: a single block sliding alone has a = g(sin θ − μₖ cos θ), and the mass cancels. It slides at constant speed when tan θ = μₖ.

Free-body diagram checklist (Q5a, 3 marks)

  • One separate diagram per mass, the mass drawn as a dot or box.
  • Every arrow starts on the body and is labelled (m₁g, N, T, fₖ = μₖN).
  • For m₁ you may show m₁g split into m₁g sin θ and m₁g cos θ.
  • Friction points opposite to the motion. Here m₁ moves down, so friction acts up the slope.
  • Show the acceleration direction beside each diagram.

WorkedQ5 worked: m₁ slides down the rough slope; m₂ hangs vertically and rises

Free-body diagrams:

  • m₁: m₁g straight down; N perpendicular out of the slope; T up the slope; fₖ up the slope; a down the slope.
  • m₂: T up; m₂g down; a up.

Perpendicular to the slope for m₁: N − m₁g cos θ = 0, so N = m₁g cos θ and fₖ = μₖm₁g cos θ.

Along the slope for m₁ (down positive): m₁g sin θ − T − μₖm₁g cos θ = m₁a ...(1)

Vertical for m₂ (up positive): T − m₂g = m₂a ...(2)

Add (1) and (2) to remove T: m₁g sin θ − μₖm₁g cos θ − m₂g = (m₁ + m₂)a

\[a=\frac{g\,(m_1\sin\theta-\mu_k m_1\cos\theta-m_2)}{m_1+m_2}\]

Tension (if asked): T = m₂(g + a).

Sense checks examiners like: if μₖ = 0 and m₂ = 0, a = g sin θ (frictionless slope). If the top of the fraction is negative, m₁ cannot move down; the question's assumption fails.

Other set-ups: if m₁ moves up the slope instead, friction acts down and a = g(m₂ − m₁ sin θ − μₖm₁ cos θ) / (m₁ + m₂). With your lab numbers (θ = 30°, m₁ = 2 kg, μₖ = 0.3, m₂ = 3 kg) this gives a = 2.9 m/s² and T = 20.7 N.

checks.q: A block rests on an incline at angle θ with no other forces pushing it into the slope. The normal reaction is:
checks.x: Perpendicular to the slope, N balances the weight component into the surface, mg cos θ.

checks.q: The Earth pulls a book down with its weight. What is the Newton's third-law partner of this force?
o: The book pulling the Earth up
The table pushing the book up
The book pushing the table down
checks.x: A third-law pair acts on different bodies and is the same type of force. The table's normal force acts on the same book, so it is not the pair.

checks.q: A block slides down a rough 30° incline at constant speed. What is μₖ?
checks.x: Constant speed means a = 0, so mg sin θ = μₖ mg cos θ and μₖ = tan 30° = 0.58.

sections.title: Apparent weight in a lift and the work-energy principle (Q6)
sections.html:
A bathroom scale reads the normal force N, not your true weight. In an accelerating lift N changes; the scale then shows N / g as a "mass".

Apparent weight: free-body diagram on the person

Only two forces: N up (from the scale) and mg down. Newton's second law with up as positive: N − mg = ma.

Lift motion Acceleration Scale reads Feels
At rest or constant velocity 0 N = mg normal
Speeding up going up up N = m(g + a) heavier
Slowing down going down up N = m(g + a) heavier
Speeding up going down down N = m(g − a) lighter
Slowing down going up (stopping at a higher floor) down N = m(g − a) lighter
Free fall (cable snaps) g down N = 0 weightless

The key word is the direction of the acceleration, not the direction of travel. Your Elevator Overload Lab shows this on its scale display.

WorkedQ6(a) worked: 70 kg person; lift went up from the ground floor and is stopping at the 2nd floor with |a| = 2 m/s²

  • Travelling up and slowing down, so the acceleration is downwards.
  • Free-body diagram: N up, mg = 686 N down, a = 2 m/s² down.
  • Up positive: N − mg = m(−a), so N = m(g − a) = 70(9.8 − 2) = 546 N.
  • The scale shows N / g = 546 / 9.8 = 55.7 kg.

Work-energy principle

The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ½mv² − ½mu².

  • Work by a constant force: W = Fd cos θ (θ between force and displacement).
  • Gravity does positive work mgh when the body falls h, negative when it rises.
  • Friction always does negative work: −fd.
  • Only gravity acting → this is the same as conservation of mechanical energy: ½mu² + mgh₁ = ½mv² + mgh₂.

WorkedQ6(b) worked: starts at 6 m with 3 m/s downwards; find v at 2 m

  • The body falls h = 6 − 2 = 4 m, so gravity does W = mg(4).
  • mg(4) = ½mv² − ½m(3)². The mass cancels.
  • v² = 3² + 2(9.8)(4) = 9 + 78.4 = 87.4
  • v = √87.4 = 9.3 m/s downwards (9.35)

Check with kinematics: v² = u² + 2as = 9 + 2(9.8)(4) gives the same answer. Use it to check, but write the energy method because the question asks for it.

checks.q: A lift is moving down and slowing down. The scale under you reads:
checks.x: Slowing a downward motion needs an upward acceleration, so N = m(g + a) > mg.

checks.q: A 60 kg student stands in a lift accelerating upwards at 2.0 m/s². What force does the floor exert? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A stone is dropped from rest from 5.0 m. Using energy, how fast is it moving at the ground?

sections.title: Momentum and collisions (Q7)
sections.html:
In every collision with no external force, total momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision; that is the test.

Key ideas

  • Momentum p = mv, a vector. Pick a positive direction (east = +) and give every velocity its sign.
  • Impulse = FΔt = Δp = mv − mu.
  • Conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
  • Convert grams to kilograms first (300 g = 0.3 kg).
Type Momentum Kinetic energy Example
Elastic conserved conserved ideal gas molecules, ideal snooker balls
Inelastic conserved some lost (heat, sound, deformation) most real collisions
Perfectly inelastic conserved maximum loss; bodies stick together ballistic pendulum, your Experiment 3

Coefficient of restitution e = (speed of separation) / (speed of approach) = (v₂ − v₁) / (u₁ − u₂). e = 1 elastic, 0 < e < 1 inelastic, e = 0 stick together. Use it as a second check.

WorkedQ7 worked: 0.3 kg at 8 m/s east hits 0.2 kg at 6 m/s west; after, 0.3 kg moves 2 m/s west

East positive: u₁ = +8, u₂ = −6, v₁ = −2, v₂ = ?

(a) Momentum before = (0.3)(8) + (0.2)(−6) = 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.2 kg·m/s Momentum after = (0.3)(−2) + 0.2v₂ = −0.6 + 0.2v₂ 1.2 = −0.6 + 0.2v₂, so v₂ = 1.8 / 0.2 = 9.0 m/s, eastwards (positive sign = east)

(b) KE before = ½(0.3)(8²) + ½(0.2)(6²) = 9.6 + 3.6 = 13.2 J KE after = ½(0.3)(2²) + ½(0.2)(9²) = 0.6 + 8.1 = 8.7 J

KE after < KE before (4.5 J lost), so the collision is inelastic, not elastic.

Check: e = (9 − (−2)) / (8 − (−6)) = 11 / 14 = 0.79, which is less than 1, so inelastic.

Trap: squaring removes the sign, so KE never needs signs; momentum always does. Forgetting the minus on the 6 m/s gives a wrong v₂.

checks.q: In a collision with no external force, which quantity is ALWAYS conserved?
checks.x: Momentum is always conserved. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

checks.q: A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Their common speed is:
checks.x: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s. After: 3.0v = 6.0, so v = 2.0 m/s.

checks.q: Two bodies stick together after colliding. The coefficient of restitution e is:
checks.x: Sticking together means zero speed of separation, so e = 0: perfectly inelastic.

sections.title: Plane mirrors and multiple images (Q8)
sections.html:
A plane mirror forms an image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Every image can act as a new object for the other mirror, which is how two facing mirrors make a long row of images.

Laws of reflection

  1. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
  2. Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

Characteristics of a plane-mirror image (Q8a: any four)

  • Virtual: it cannot be caught on a screen; rays only appear to come from it.
  • Upright (erect).
  • Same size as the object (magnification = 1).
  • Same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
  • Laterally inverted (left and right swapped).
  • The line joining object and image is perpendicular to the mirror.

Useful extras: if the mirror moves d, the image moves 2d. Two mirrors at angle θ give n = 360°/θ − 1 images (when 360/θ is even).

Two parallel mirrors: the method

Put a number line along the floor: M₁ at 0, M₂ at D, the person O at x (between them). Reflecting a point at position p:

  • in M₁ (at 0) gives −p
  • in M₂ (at D) gives 2D − p

Keep reflecting each image in the opposite mirror.

WorkedQ8(b) worked: M₁ on the left, M₂ on the right, separation D; O is x from M₁

Image How it is formed Position Distance from its mirror
1st image in M₁ (I₁) O reflected in M₁ −x x behind M₁
1st image in M₂ (I₁′) O reflected in M₂ 2D − x D − x behind M₂
2nd image in M₁ (I₂) I₁′ reflected in M₁ −(2D − x) = x − 2D 2D − x behind M₁
2nd image in M₂ (I₂′) I₁ reflected in M₂ 2D − (−x) = 2D + x D + x behind M₂

Distance between the second images = (2D + x) − (x − 2D) = 4D.

The answer does not depend on x: wherever the person stands, the two second images are always 4D apart.

Sketch for the marks: two vertical lines (M₁, M₂) D apart; O at x from M₁; I₁ at x behind M₁; I₁′ at D − x behind M₂; I₂ at 2D − x behind M₁; I₂′ at D + x behind M₂; label each distance and the total 4D.

Check with numbers: D = 3 m, x = 1 m. Positions: I₂ at −5, I₂′ at 7; gap 12 m = 4 × 3 ✓.

checks.q: Which of these is NOT true of the image in a plane mirror?
o: It is the same size as the object
checks.x: A plane-mirror image is virtual: the rays only appear to come from behind the mirror, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

checks.q: You stand still and a plane mirror is moved 0.5 m away from you. How far does your image move?
checks.x: If the mirror moves d, the image moves 2d.

checks.q: How many images do you see between two plane mirrors at 60° to each other?

sections.title: Spherical mirrors (Q9)
sections.html:
One equation does every mirror question; the marks are in the signs. A convex mirror always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image.

Terms: pole P (centre of the mirror surface), centre of curvature C, radius R, principal axis, principal focus F, focal length f = R/2.

\[\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}\qquad m=\frac{h_i}{h_o}=-\frac{v}{u}\]

Sign convention (real-is-positive, the usual one in first-year physics)

Quantity Positive (+) Negative (−)
u (object distance) real object, in front virtual object
v (image distance) real image, in front of the mirror virtual image, behind the mirror
f concave (converging) mirror convex (diverging) mirror
m upright image inverted image

|m| > 1 magnified, |m| < 1 diminished. If your lecturer used the Cartesian (new) convention instead, the formula and signs change but the physical answer (where the image is, upright or not, size) is the same. State the convention you use at the start of your answer.

Images in a concave mirror (object moving in from far away)

Object position Image position Nature
Beyond C between F and C real, inverted, diminished
At C at C real, inverted, same size
Between C and F beyond C real, inverted, magnified
At F at infinity no image formed
Between F and P behind the mirror virtual, upright, magnified (shaving or makeup mirror)

Convex mirror, any object position: image behind the mirror, between P and F; virtual, upright, diminished. Used as car side mirrors and shop security mirrors because of the wide field of view.

Ray rules for sketches: a ray parallel to the axis reflects through F (concave) or as if from F (convex); a ray towards F (or C) reflects back parallel (or back on itself); a ray to P reflects at an equal angle.

WorkedQ9 worked: object 6 cm in front of a convex mirror, |f| = 12 cm

(a) Convex, so f = −12 cm; u = +6 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/12 − 1/6 = −1/12 − 2/12 = −3/12 = −1/4 v = −4.0 cm: the image is 4.0 cm behind the mirror.

(b) m = −v/u = −(−4)/6 = +0.7 (0.67)

(c) Any two, each with its reason:

  • Virtual, because v is negative (the image is behind the mirror).
  • Upright, because m is positive.
  • Diminished (two-thirds the object's height), because |m| = 0.67 < 1.

Check with the Cartesian convention (u = −6, f = +12, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f): 1/v = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4, v = +4 cm (behind), m = −v/u = +0.67. Same image.

checks.q: A convex mirror ALWAYS gives an image that is:
checks.x: For any object position a convex (diverging) mirror forms the image behind the mirror, between P and F.

checks.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with f = 10 cm. Where is the image? (real-is-positive)
o: 15 cm in front of the mirror
7.5 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror
checks.x: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so v = +15 cm: real, in front of the mirror. m = −15/30 = −0.5, inverted and diminished.

checks.q: An object is placed exactly at the focus of a concave mirror. The image is:
o: at infinity, so no image is formed
checks.x: Rays from F reflect parallel and never meet.

sections.title: Refraction and apparent depth (Q10)
sections.html:
Light bends at a boundary because its speed changes. An object under a transparent layer looks closer to the surface than it is: apparent depth a = (n₂/n₁)h, and the image is raised by d = h(1 − n₂/n₁).

Key facts

  • Refractive index n = c / v, where v is the speed of light in the material. n ≥ 1; air ≈ 1.00.
  • Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (angles from the normal).
  • Going into a denser medium (larger n) the ray bends towards the normal; into a less dense medium it bends away.
  • Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change: λ_medium = λ_vacuum / n.
  • Critical angle (dense to less dense): sin C = n₂/n₁. Beyond C → total internal reflection (optical fibres).

Q10(a) worked: v = c / n₁ = (3.0 × 10⁸) / 1.36 = 2.2 × 10⁸ m/s

Q10(b) labelled diagram (2 marks)

Draw it like this:

  1. A horizontal line for the top surface, material of index n₁ below (thickness h), air n₂ above.
  2. Object O on the bottom; a vertical normal from O straight up through point N on the surface.
  3. A ray from O to point B on the surface a short distance x from N; angle θ₁ between the ray and the normal at B.
  4. The ray leaves into air bent away from the normal, at angle θ₂ > θ₁.
  5. Extend the air ray backwards (dashed) until it meets the vertical line above O at I, the image.
  6. Label NO = h (real depth), NI = a (apparent depth), OI = d (displacement from the bottom), and NB = x.

WorkedQ10(c) worked: derive a and d (6 marks)

From triangle ONB: tan θ₁ = x / h From triangle INB: tan θ₂ = x / a (the angle at I equals θ₂ because the normals are parallel)

Snell's law at B: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

Small angles, so sin θ ≈ tan θ: n₁ (x / h) = n₂ (x / a)

Cancel x and rearrange:

\[a=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\,h \qquad d=h-a=h\left(1-\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)\]

In air n₂ = 1, so a = h / n₁ (real depth ÷ apparent depth = n). With n₁ = 1.36: a = 0.74h and d = 0.26h, so the object appears raised by about a quarter of the thickness.

Everyday examples: a pool looks shallower than it is; a straw looks bent in water; a coin under a glass block looks lifted.

checks.q: Light passes from air into glass. The ray bends:
checks.x: Going into a denser medium (larger n) the light slows down and bends towards the normal.

checks.q: Glass has n = 1.5. What is the speed of light in it? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
A pool is 2.0 m deep and water has n = 1.33. Looking straight down, the pool seems to be:
checks.x: Apparent depth a = h / n = 2.0 / 1.33 = 1.5 m. The bottom looks raised by about 0.5 m.

checks.q: When light enters water from air, which property stays the same?
checks.x: Frequency is set by the source. Speed and wavelength both drop by the factor n.

One-page formula sheet

Topic Formulas
Kinematics (constant a) v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t
Projectiles uₓ = u cos θ, uᵧ = u sin θ; x = uₓt; y = uᵧt − ½gt²; R = u² sin 2θ / g; H = u² sin² θ / 2g; T = 2u sin θ / g
Vectors Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ (θ from x-axis);
Newton ΣF = ma; weight W = mg; fₖ = μₖN; fₛ ≤ μₛN; on a slope N = mg cos θ, pull down slope = mg sin θ
Lift N = m(g + a) accelerating up; N = m(g − a) accelerating down; scale mass = N / g
Work and energy W = Fd cos θ; KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; W_net = ΔKE; P = W / t = Fv

Spherical mirrors 1/u + 1/v = 1/f; f = R/2; m = −v/u (real-is-positive)
Refraction n = c/v; n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; apparent depth a = (n₂/n₁)h; sin C = n₂/n₁

Answers to the whole 2024/25 paper at a glance

Q Final answers

3 D × E = −23î + 17ĵ + 22k̂ (both dot products = 0)

Traps checklist (tick off before handing in)

  • Angle from the y-axis? Then x uses sin, y uses cos.
  • Vector direction found from a sketch, not the calculator alone.
  • Cross product: minus sign on the middle (ĵ) term; checked with dot products.
  • Projectile: time from the horizontal motion, then height from the vertical.
  • Friction drawn opposite to the motion, on its own free-body diagram per mass.
  • Lift: used the direction of acceleration, not of travel (stopping going up = lighter).
  • Momentum: velocities carry signs; grams converted to kg.
  • Elastic test done with kinetic energy, not momentum.
  • Mirror: sign convention stated; convex f negative.
  • Final answers rounded to one decimal place, with units.

From your labs (examinable ideas): ballistic pendulum (momentum conserved in the collision, energy only after it: v₀ = ((M + m)/m)√(2gL(1 − cos θ))); spring (T = 2π√(m/k), so k = 4π² / gradient of T² against M); friction incline (a = g(sin θ − μₖ cos θ); constant speed when tan θ = μₖ).

sets.title: 2024/25 final, fully worked
sets.desc: All ten questions from last year's paper. Try each one, then reveal the working step by step.

qs.label: Q1
qs.q: Show that the equation v = √(2(P − P₀)/ρ + 2gh) is dimensionally correct, where v is a speed, P and P₀ are pressures, ρ is a density, g is the acceleration due to gravity and h is a height.
steps: [v] = L T⁻¹
[P − P₀] = M L T⁻² / L² = M L⁻¹ T⁻²
[ρ] = M L⁻³
First term: (M L⁻¹ T⁻²) / (M L⁻³) = L² T⁻²
Second term: [g][h] = (L T⁻²)(L) = L² T⁻²
Both terms are L² T⁻², so adding them is valid.
RHS = √(L² T⁻²) = L T⁻¹ = LHS.
Conclusion: the equation is dimensionally correct. (It is a form of Bernoulli's equation.)

qs.label: Q2
qs.q:
Vector A has magnitude 15 units at 40° above the −x axis. Vector B has magnitude 10 units at 20° from the −y axis, pointing down and to the left.
(a) Write A and B in unit-vector form.
(b) Find C = A − 2B.
(c) Sketch C and find its magnitude and its direction from the +x axis.
steps: (a) A points up-left (2nd quadrant), angle from the x-axis: A = −15 cos 40° î + 15 sin 40° ĵ = −11.5î + 9.6ĵ
B points down-left (3rd quadrant), angle from the y-axis, so sin goes with x: B = −10 sin 20° î − 10 cos 20° ĵ = −3.4î − 9.4ĵ
(c) Sketch C in the 2nd quadrant, long and leaning slightly left of the +y axis. |C| = √(4.65² + 28.44²) = 28.8 units α = tan⁻¹(28.44 / 4.65) = 80.7°, so θ = 180° − 80.7° = 99.3° from the +x axis.
Check: 99.3° is just past 90°, which matches a vector pointing almost straight up and slightly left.

qs.label: Q3
qs.q: D = 2î + 4ĵ − k̂ and E = −3î + 5ĵ − 7k̂. Find a vector perpendicular to both D and E, and prove that it is perpendicular to both.
steps: D × E = −23î + 17ĵ + 22k̂
Prove it (always do this, it earns marks and catches sign errors)
Both dot products are zero, so the vector is perpendicular to D and E.

The question says "one of the vectors": E × D = 23î − 17ĵ − 22k̂, or any multiple, is also correct. If asked for a unit vector: |D × E| = √(529 + 289 + 484) = √1302 = 36.1, so n̂ = (−23î + 17ĵ + 22k̂) / 36.1.

qs.label: Q4
qs.q:
A girl stands 2.5 m from the wall of a house. She throws a ball from 1.4 m above the ground at 5 m/s, 60° above the horizontal. A window in the wall runs from 0.6 m to 1.6 m above the ground.
(a) Sketch the situation.
(b) Find the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity.
(c) How long does the ball take to reach the wall?
(d) Does the ball go through the window?
steps: (a) Sketch: ground line; the girl's release point 1.4 m up; the house wall 2.5 m away; window marked from 0.60 m to 1.60 m (0.60 + 1.0) on the wall; a parabola from the release point to the wall.
(b) uₓ = 5 cos 60° = 2.5 m/s; uᵧ = 5 sin 60° = 4.3 m/s (4.33)
(c) t = 2.5 / 2.5 = 1.0 s
The window runs from 0.60 m to 1.60 m, and 0.60 < 0.83 < 1.60, so the ball hits the window, about 0.23 m above its base.
Check: the ball peaks at t = 4.33 / 9.8 = 0.44 s at 1.4 + 4.33² / 19.6 = 2.36 m, then comes down. At 1.0 s it is on the way down but still above the ground, so the answer is consistent.

qs.label: Q5
qs.q:
Mass m₁ sits on a rough plane inclined at θ (coefficient of kinetic friction μₖ). A light string runs over a smooth pulley at the top to a mass m₂ hanging vertically. m₁ slides down the slope and m₂ rises.
(a) Draw a free-body diagram for each mass.
(b) Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system.
steps: Free-body diagrams:
m₁: m₁g straight down; N perpendicular out of the slope; T up the slope; fₖ up the slope; a down the slope.
m₂: T up; m₂g down; a up.
Perpendicular to the slope for m₁: N − m₁g cos θ = 0, so N = m₁g cos θ and fₖ = μₖm₁g cos θ.
Along the slope for m₁ (down positive): m₁g sin θ − T − μₖm₁g cos θ = m₁a ...(1)
Vertical for m₂ (up positive): T − m₂g = m₂a ...(2)
Add (1) and (2) to remove T: m₁g sin θ − μₖm₁g cos θ − m₂g = (m₁ + m₂)a
\[a=\frac{g\,(m_1\sin\theta-\mu_k m_1\cos\theta-m_2)}{m_1+m_2}\]
Tension (if asked): T = m₂(g + a).

qs.label: Q6a
qs.q: A 70 kg person stands on a bathroom scale in a lift. The lift went up from the ground floor and is now slowing down to stop at the 2nd floor with an acceleration of magnitude 2 m/s². Find the normal force on the person and the mass the scale shows.
steps: Travelling up and slowing down, so the acceleration is downwards.
Free-body diagram: N up, mg = 686 N down, a = 2 m/s² down.
Up positive: N − mg = m(−a), so N = m(g − a) = 70(9.8 − 2) = 546 N.
The scale shows N / g = 546 / 9.8 = 55.7 kg.

qs.label: Q6b
qs.q: Using the work–energy principle: a body 6 m above the ground is moving downwards at 3 m/s. Find its speed when it is 2 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance.
steps: The body falls h = 6 − 2 = 4 m, so gravity does W = mg(4).
mg(4) = ½mv² − ½m(3)². The mass cancels.
v = √87.4 = 9.3 m/s downwards (9.35)
Check with kinematics: v² = u² + 2as = 9 + 2(9.8)(4) gives the same answer. Use it to check, but write the energy method because the question asks for it.

qs.label: Q7
qs.q:
A 0.3 kg ball moving at 8 m/s east collides head-on with a 0.2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s west. After the collision the 0.3 kg ball moves at 2 m/s west.
(a) Find the velocity of the 0.2 kg ball after the collision.
(b) Is the collision elastic? Show your working.
steps: East positive: u₁ = +8, u₂ = −6, v₁ = −2, v₂ = ?
(a) Momentum before = (0.3)(8) + (0.2)(−6) = 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.2 kg·m/s Momentum after = (0.3)(−2) + 0.2v₂ = −0.6 + 0.2v₂ 1.2 = −0.6 + 0.2v₂, so v₂ = 1.8 / 0.2 = 9.0 m/s, eastwards (positive sign = east)
(b) KE before = ½(0.3)(8²) + ½(0.2)(6²) = 9.6 + 3.6 = 13.2 J KE after = ½(0.3)(2²) + ½(0.2)(9²) = 0.6 + 8.1 = 8.7 J
KE after < KE before (4.5 J lost), so the collision is inelastic, not elastic.
Check: e = (9 − (−2)) / (8 − (−6)) = 11 / 14 = 0.79, which is less than 1, so inelastic.

qs.label: Q8b
qs.q: Two plane mirrors M₁ and M₂ face each other a distance D apart. A person O stands between them, a distance x from M₁. Find the distance between the second image formed in M₁ and the second image formed in M₂.
steps:
Image How it is formed Position Distance from its mirror
1st image in M₁ (I₁) O reflected in M₁ −x x behind M₁
1st image in M₂ (I₁′) O reflected in M₂ 2D − x D − x behind M₂
2nd image in M₁ (I₂) I₁′ reflected in M₁ −(2D − x) = x − 2D 2D − x behind M₁
2nd image in M₂ (I₂′) I₁ reflected in M₂ 2D − (−x) = 2D + x D + x behind M₂
Distance between the second images = (2D + x) − (x − 2D) = 4D.
The answer does not depend on x: wherever the person stands, the two second images are always 4D apart.

Sketch for the marks: two vertical lines (M₁, M₂) D apart; O at x from M₁; I₁ at x behind M₁; I₁′ at D − x behind M₂; I₂ at 2D − x behind M₁; I₂′ at D + x behind M₂; label each distance and the total 4D.
Check with numbers: D = 3 m, x = 1 m. Positions: I₂ at −5, I₂′ at 7; gap 12 m = 4 × 3 ✓.

qs.label: Q9
qs.q:
An object is placed 6 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 12 cm.
(a) Find the position of the image.
(b) Find the magnification.
(c) State two characteristics of the image, each with its reason.
steps: (a) Convex, so f = −12 cm; u = +6 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/12 − 1/6 = −1/12 − 2/12 = −3/12 = −1/4 v = −4.0 cm: the image is 4.0 cm behind the mirror.
(c) Any two, each with its reason:
Virtual, because v is negative (the image is behind the mirror).
Upright, because m is positive.
Diminished (two-thirds the object's height), because |m| = 0.67 < 1.
Check with the Cartesian convention (u = −6, f = +12, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f): 1/v = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4, v = +4 cm (behind), m = −v/u = +0.67. Same image.

qs.label: Q10
qs.q:
An object lies at the bottom of a transparent block of thickness h and refractive index n₁ = 1.36. It is viewed from air (index n₂) almost straight above.
(a) Find the speed of light in the block.
(b) Draw a labelled ray diagram showing the real and apparent depths.
(c) Using small angles, derive the apparent depth a and the apparent displacement d.
steps: Q10(b) labelled diagram (2 marks)
Draw it like this:
A horizontal line for the top surface, material of index n₁ below (thickness h), air n₂ above.
Object O on the bottom; a vertical normal from O straight up through point N on the surface.
A ray from O to point B on the surface a short distance x from N; angle θ₁ between the ray and the normal at B.
The ray leaves into air bent away from the normal, at angle θ₂ > θ₁.
Extend the air ray backwards (dashed) until it meets the vertical line above O at I, the image.
Label NO = h (real depth), NI = a (apparent depth), OI = d (displacement from the bottom), and NB = x.

WorkedQ10(c) worked: derive a and d (6 marks)

From triangle ONB: tan θ₁ = x / h From triangle INB: tan θ₂ = x / a (the angle at I equals θ₂ because the normals are parallel)

Snell's law at B: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

Small angles, so sin θ ≈ tan θ: n₁ (x / h) = n₂ (x / a)

Cancel x and rearrange:

\[a=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\,h \qquad d=h-a=h\left(1-\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)\]

In air n₂ = 1, so a = h / n₁ (real depth ÷ apparent depth = n). With n₁ = 1.36: a = 0.74h and d = 0.26h, so the object appears raised by about a quarter of the thickness.

qs.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward from ground level at 14.7 m s⁻¹. Calculate (a) the maximum height it reaches; (b) the total time it is in the air before landing back at the point of projection.
qs.hint: At the top v = 0: use v² = u² − 2gh. Time up = u/g, and the flight is twice that.
qs.label: A1

qs.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ from the roof of a building 45 m high. On the way down it just misses the edge of the roof. Determine (a) the maximum height above the ground; (b) the time to reach the maximum height; (c) the velocity and position relative to the point of projection 3.0 s after it is thrown; (d) the total time in the air; (e) the velocity with which it hits the ground.
qs.ans: (a) 64.6 m above the ground (b) 2.0 s (c) 9.8 m s⁻¹ downward, 14.7 m above the point of projection (d) 5.63 s (e) 35.6 m s⁻¹ downward

(a) Sketch the velocity–time graph of the sandbag until it lands (up positive, key values marked). (b) Calculate the maximum height above the ground reached by the sandbag. (c) Calculate the time to reach the ground and the impact speed.
qs.ans: (a) A straight line from +4.9 m s⁻¹ at t = 0, crossing zero at 0.5 s and reaching −24.5 m s⁻¹ at 3.0 s (gradient −9.8 m s⁻²). (b) 30.6 m (c) 3.0 s and 24.5 m s⁻¹

qs.q: A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge 44.1 m above a river. 1.5 s later a second stone is thrown vertically downward from the same point. Both hit the water at the same instant. Calculate (a) the time for the first stone to reach the water; (b) the initial speed of the second stone; (c) the speed of each stone as it hits the water.
qs.ans: (a) 3.0 s (b) 22.1 m s⁻¹ (c) 29.4 m s⁻¹ (first), 36.8 m s⁻¹ (second)
qs.hint: The second stone has 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5 s to fall the same 44.1 m.
qs.label: A4

qs.q: A flower pot falls from rest from a window ledge. A person in a room below sees it pass a 2.0 m tall window in 0.25 s. How far above the top of the window was the pot released?
qs.hint: Find the speed at the top of the window from 2.0 = u(0.25) + ½(9.8)(0.25)², then use v² = 2gh.
qs.label: A5

qs.q: A marble rolls horizontally off a table 1.25 m high and lands 2.0 m from the foot of the table. Calculate (a) its speed as it leaves the table; (b) the magnitude and direction of its velocity just before it hits the floor.
qs.ans: (a) 3.96 m s⁻¹ (b) 6.34 m s⁻¹ at 51.3° below the horizontal
qs.label: B1

qs.q: A ball thrown from 1.5 m above the ground must enter a window 6.4 m above the ground moving horizontally only. The window is 5.0 m horizontally from the point of projection. Find the speed and direction of projection.
qs.ans: 11.0 m s⁻¹ at 63.0° above the horizontal (uₓ = 5.0, uᵧ = 9.8 m s⁻¹)
qs.hint: Moving horizontally means it is at the top of its path: vᵧ = 0 after rising 4.9 m.
qs.label: B2

qs.q: A stone is projected at 30° above the horizontal from the top of a building 15 m high. It just clears a wall 19.4 m high, 24 m horizontally from the point of projection. Calculate (a) the initial speed u; (b) the vertical velocity as it clears the wall, and whether it is moving up or down; (c) the time to hit the ground; (d) the horizontal distance to where it lands.
qs.ans: (a) u ≈ 20.0 m s⁻¹ (b) vᵧ = −3.6 m s⁻¹, moving downwards (c) 3.05 s (d) 52.8 m
qs.label: B3

qs.q: Two objects are projected towards each other from ground-level points A and B, 30 m apart, with the same speed: the one from A at 40°, the one from B at 55°. Their ranges overlap by 6 m. Find the common projection speed and the ranges R(A) and R(B).
qs.hint: R(A) + R(B) = 30 + 6 = 36 m, and each R = u² sin 2θ / g.
qs.label: B4

qs.q: A worker pushes a 12.5 kg crate across a frictionless floor with a constant horizontal 15 N force. Starting from rest, how far does it move in 4.0 s?
qs.group: Section C · Newton's laws, impulse and equilibrium (MC6)
qs.label: C1

qs.q: A 2.0 kg puck on ice feels three forces: F₁ = (4i + 3j) N, F₂ = (−i + 2j) N and F₃ = (3i − j) N. (a) Find the magnitude and direction of its acceleration. (b) What fourth force would keep it moving at constant velocity?
qs.ans: (a) 3.61 m s⁻² at 33.7° above the +x axis (b) F₄ = (−6i − 4j) N
qs.group: Section C · Newton's laws, impulse and equilibrium (MC6)
qs.label: C2

qs.q: A 150 g tennis ball at 20 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 30 m s⁻¹. Contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the impulse on the ball and the average force from the racket, with directions.
qs.ans: 7.5 N s and 150 N, both in the direction of the ball's return
qs.hint: Take the return direction as positive: the initial velocity is −20 m s⁻¹.

qs.label: C3

qs.q: A light rope ABCD hangs from fixed points A and D. m₁ = 10 kg hangs from B and an unknown m₂ from C. In equilibrium BC is horizontal, AB makes 45° with the horizontal and CD makes 60°. Find the tensions in AB, BC and CD, and m₂.
qs.hint: Resolve at B first: vertical gives T(AB) sin 45° = m₁g.
qs.group: Section C · Newton's laws, impulse and equilibrium (MC6)
qs.label: C4

qs.q: An 8.0 kg trolley rests on a floor with coefficient of friction 0.25. A person applies 50 N. (a) Pushing at 25° below the horizontal, how far does it move in 3.0 s from rest? (b) Pulling at 25° above the horizontal, how far in 3.0 s? (c) Why do the answers differ?
qs.ans: Push: N = 99.5 N, a = 2.55 m s⁻², 11.5 m. Pull: N = 57.3 N, a = 3.87 m s⁻², 17.4 m. Pushing down raises the normal reaction, so friction is larger.
qs.group: Section C · Newton's laws, impulse and equilibrium (MC6)
qs.label: C5

qs.q: A 70 kg student stands on a scale in a lift going up. The lift accelerates up at 1.5 m s⁻², moves at constant velocity, then slows to a stop at 2.0 m s⁻². Find the scale reading while it (a) speeds up; (b) moves steadily; (c) slows down.
qs.group: Section D · Connected bodies, lifts and work–energy (MC7)
qs.label: D1

qs.q: A 2.5 kg block starts at the top of a rough 25° incline at 3.0 m s⁻¹. After sliding 4.0 m down it moves at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Using work–energy, find (a) the coefficient of kinetic friction; (b) the work done against friction.
qs.group: Section D · Connected bodies, lifts and work–energy (MC7)
qs.label: D2

qs.q: ABC is a smooth track and CD a rough horizontal surface. A 3.0 kg object leaves A (25 m up) at 3.0 m s⁻¹, passes the lowest point B (5 m up), rises to C (15 m up) and slides along CD until it stops; μ on CD = 0.30. Find (a) the speed at B; (b) the speed at C; (c) the distance along CD before stopping.
qs.group: Section D · Connected bodies, lifts and work–energy (MC7)
qs.label: D3

qs.q: m₁ = 8.0 kg rests on a rough plane at 30°, joined over a light frictionless pulley to a hanging mass m₂; μₛ = 0.35 and μₖ = 0.25. (a) Derive the acceleration and tension when m₁ slides UP the incline. (b) Find the largest m₂ that will not make m₁ move up. (c) Find the smallest m₂ that stops m₁ sliding down. (d) If m₂ = 10 kg, find the acceleration and tension.
qs.ans: (a) a = [m₂g − m₁g(sin θ + μₖ cos θ)] / (m₁ + m₂), T = m₂(g − a) (b) 6.43 kg (c) 1.58 kg (d) a = 2.32 m s⁻², T = 74.8 N
qs.group: Section D · Connected bodies, lifts and work–energy (MC7)
qs.label: D4

qs.q: m₁ = 400 g on a rough horizontal surface is joined over a frictionless pulley to m₂ = 600 g on an incline (μₖ = 0.30 between m₂ and the incline). At θ = 35° the masses move at constant speed with m₂ sliding down. (a) Find μₖ between m₁ and the horizontal surface. (b) If θ is raised to 45°, find the acceleration and tension.
qs.group: Section D · Connected bodies, lifts and work–energy (MC7)
qs.label: D5

qs.q: A 60 kg skater at rest on smooth ice throws a 2.0 kg ball forward at 12 m s⁻¹. Find the skater's recoil velocity.
qs.ans: 0.40 m s⁻¹, opposite to the ball
qs.label: E1

qs.q: Trolleys of 4.0 kg and 2.0 kg move east at 8.0 and 2.0 m s⁻¹. They collide perfectly elastically and both continue east at v₃ (≠ 8.0) and v₄ (≠ 2.0). Find v₃ and v₄ and show kinetic energy is conserved.
qs.ans: v₃ = 4.0 m s⁻¹, v₄ = 10.0 m s⁻¹; KE = 132 J before and after
qs.label: E2

qs.q: A 20 g bullet at 600 m s⁻¹ embeds in a 2.98 kg block at the edge of a table. The block lands 2.0 m from the table. Find (a) the height of the table; (b) the percentage of the bullet's kinetic energy lost in the collision.
qs.ans: Common velocity 4.0 m s⁻¹, fall time 0.50 s, (a) h = 1.23 m (b) 99.3 % lost
qs.label: E3

qs.q: A 300 g object at 4.0 m s⁻¹, 30° above the x-axis, collides with a second object at 5.0 m s⁻¹, 45° below the x-axis. They stick together and move along the x-axis. Find (a) the mass of the second object; (b) the speed after the collision; (c) the kinetic energy lost.
qs.hint: Along the x-axis afterwards means the total y-momentum is zero.
qs.label: E4

qs.q: A 75 kg man swings on a rope from a tree house 12 m up, grabs a 50 kg woman at the lowest point, and hopes to reach a branch 6 m up. (a) What maximum height can they reach if he starts from rest? (b) What minimum initial speed must he have?
qs.hint: Energy down to the bottom, momentum in the grab, energy back up.

sets.title: Quick checks
sets.desc: Short multiple-choice questions on every topic in the notes, with the reason for each answer.

qs.q: What are the dimensions of pressure?
qs.x: Pressure = force / area = (M L T⁻²) / L² = M L⁻¹ T⁻².

qs.q: A spring constant is k = F / x. What are its dimensions?
qs.x: (M L T⁻²) / L = M T⁻². The L cancels.

qs.q: Which mistake can dimensional analysis NOT catch?
o: Writing 2 instead of ½ in front of a term
Adding a speed to an acceleration
Using L² where L is needed
Leaving out a factor of time
qs.x: Pure numbers are dimensionless, so a wrong constant leaves the dimensions unchanged. A correct check means consistent, not definitely true.

qs.q: A vector of size A makes angle θ with the y-axis. What is its x-component (before signs)?
qs.x: When the angle is from the y-axis the roles swap: x uses sin, y uses cos.

qs.q: R = −3î + 4ĵ. What is its direction measured from the +x axis?
qs.x: Reference angle tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1°. R points up-left (2nd quadrant), so θ = 180° − 53.1° = 126.9°. |R| = 5.

qs.q: A vector points down and to the left. Which signs do its components have?
qs.x: Down-left is the 3rd quadrant: both components negative.
Multiply matching components and add: (2)(4) + (3)(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5. A dot product is a number.

qs.q: What is ĵ × î?
qs.x: Forwards round the cycle î → ĵ → k̂ gives +. ĵ × î goes backwards, so it is −k̂.

qs.q: A · B = 0 for two non-zero vectors. What does this tell you?
o: One of them is a unit vector
qs.x: A · B = |A||B| cos θ. It is zero when cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°.

qs.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path (no air resistance):
o: vertical velocity is zero; horizontal velocity is unchanged
qs.x: Only vᵧ becomes zero. uₓ never changes, and the acceleration is still g downwards.

qs.q: A ball rolls off a table 4.9 m high at 6.0 m/s. How far from the table does it land? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
qs.x: Fall time: 4.9 = ½(9.8)t², so t = 1.0 s. Range = uₓt = 6.0 × 1.0 = 6.0 m.

qs.q: For launch and landing on the same level, which angle gives the greatest range?
qs.x: R = u² sin 2θ / g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, so 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°.

qs.q: A block rests on an incline at angle θ with no other forces pushing it into the slope. The normal reaction is:
qs.x: Perpendicular to the slope, N balances the weight component into the surface, mg cos θ.
qs.group: 5. Newton's laws, friction and connected masses (Q5)

qs.q: The Earth pulls a book down with its weight. What is the Newton's third-law partner of this force?
o: The book pulling the Earth up
The table pushing the book up
The book pushing the table down
qs.x: A third-law pair acts on different bodies and is the same type of force. The table's normal force acts on the same book, so it is not the pair.
qs.group: 5. Newton's laws, friction and connected masses (Q5)

qs.q: A block slides down a rough 30° incline at constant speed. What is μₖ?
qs.x: Constant speed means a = 0, so mg sin θ = μₖ mg cos θ and μₖ = tan 30° = 0.58.
qs.group: 5. Newton's laws, friction and connected masses (Q5)

qs.q: A lift is moving down and slowing down. The scale under you reads:
qs.x: Slowing a downward motion needs an upward acceleration, so N = m(g + a) > mg.
qs.group: 6. Apparent weight in a lift and the work-energy principle (Q6)

qs.q: A 60 kg student stands in a lift accelerating upwards at 2.0 m/s². What force does the floor exert? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
qs.group: 6. Apparent weight in a lift and the work-energy principle (Q6)

qs.q: A stone is dropped from rest from 5.0 m. Using energy, how fast is it moving at the ground?
qs.group: 6. Apparent weight in a lift and the work-energy principle (Q6)

qs.q: In a collision with no external force, which quantity is ALWAYS conserved?
qs.x: Momentum is always conserved. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

qs.q: A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Their common speed is:
qs.x: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s. After: 3.0v = 6.0, so v = 2.0 m/s.

qs.q: Two bodies stick together after colliding. The coefficient of restitution e is:
qs.x: Sticking together means zero speed of separation, so e = 0: perfectly inelastic.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT true of the image in a plane mirror?
o: It is the same size as the object
qs.x: A plane-mirror image is virtual: the rays only appear to come from behind the mirror, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

qs.q: You stand still and a plane mirror is moved 0.5 m away from you. How far does your image move?
qs.x: If the mirror moves d, the image moves 2d.

qs.q: How many images do you see between two plane mirrors at 60° to each other?
A convex mirror ALWAYS gives an image that is:
qs.x: For any object position a convex (diverging) mirror forms the image behind the mirror, between P and F.

qs.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with f = 10 cm. Where is the image? (real-is-positive)
o: 15 cm in front of the mirror
7.5 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror
qs.x: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so v = +15 cm: real, in front of the mirror. m = −15/30 = −0.5, inverted and diminished.

qs.q: An object is placed exactly at the focus of a concave mirror. The image is:
o: at infinity, so no image is formed
qs.x: Rays from F reflect parallel and never meet.

qs.q: Light passes from air into glass. The ray bends:
qs.x: Going into a denser medium (larger n) the light slows down and bends towards the normal.

qs.q: Glass has n = 1.5. What is the speed of light in it? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
A pool is 2.0 m deep and water has n = 1.33. Looking straight down, the pool seems to be:
qs.x: Apparent depth a = h / n = 2.0 / 1.33 = 1.5 m. The bottom looks raised by about 0.5 m.

qs.q: When light enters water from air, which property stays the same?
qs.x: Frequency is set by the source. Speed and wavelength both drop by the factor n.
